title: Scaling Out: Statelessness & the Scaling Cube

options.text: It never stores any data anywhere
It keeps no per-client state between requests, so any instance can serve any request

questions.explanation: Stateless means no per-client memory is kept on the server between requests; state lives in a shared store or in the request, so servers are interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Where can you move state to make a service stateless? Select all that apply.

options.text: A signed token carried by the client

questions.explanation: State can go to a shared database, a distributed cache, object storage, or travel with the client as a token. Local memory is exactly what makes a service stateful.

questions.prompt: Match each AKF Scale Cube axis to what it means.

pairs.right: Clone the whole app behind a load balancer
Split the system into separate services by function
Partition the data so each node handles a subset

questions.explanation: X duplicates the whole app, Y splits by function (services), and Z splits by data (sharding). Real systems combine all three.

questions.prompt: Which scaling axis does statelessness most directly enable?
questions.explanation: Cloning the whole app (X-axis) only works if instances are interchangeable, which requires statelessness.

questions.prompt: A service writes uploaded files to local disk. Why does this break when scaled out?

options.text: Local files are per-server state, so a follow-up request on another server won't find them
Files cannot be uploaded over HTTP
It doesn't break; local disk is shared automatically

questions.explanation: Local disk is state tied to one server. Using shared object storage keeps the service stateless so any server can serve any request.

questions.prompt: Splitting a system into separate services by function corresponds to the ______-axis of the AKF Scale Cube. (single letter)
questions.explanation: The Y-axis is functional decomposition — splitting by function into independent services, the road toward microservices.
